citation.title: Age differences in spatial working memory contributions to visuomotor adaptation and transfer

study.eligibility_rationale: Upper-extremity visuomotor rotation task with a joystick: "Three rotation magnitudes, 15◦, 30◦ and 45◦ clockwise rotations of the feedback display about the center of the screen, were presented to participants." Two age groups are compared: "Young (N = 18, 20.8 ± 2.5 years old ... ) and older adults (N = 18, 72.3 ± 4.7 years old ...)". Performance during the perturbation blocks is reported ("Performance on the task was measured by reaction time (RT), direction error (DE) and initial endpoint error (IEE)"; Figs. 1 and 2 plot BL, A1, A2, A3 and AE). Paper is in English.
study.design_notes: Repeated exposure is a central design feature: every participant adapted to three rotations in sequence with washout runs between them ("Each magnitude of visual rotation was given for three consecutive runs. Following each magnitude of visual rotation the display returned to baseline conditions for two consecutive runs for washout of the adaptation"). Only the participants' FIRST rotation qualifies as an independent first exposure. Two presentation orders split the sample into independent subgroups: "Presentation order 1 (9 young adults and 9 older adults) received the visual rotations in the order of 30◦, 15◦ and 45◦. Presentation order 2 (a separate group of 9 young adults and 9 older adults) received the visual rotations in the order of 45◦, 15◦ and 30◦." Hence the 30° first exposure comes only from order 1 and the 45° first exposure only from order 2; the 15° rotation was never first and is not plotted. Figs. 1 and 2 each plot two symbol series per panel (grey squares and black diamonds), which correspond to the initial (learning) versus last (transfer) exposure / presentation orders; the second pass must establish from the figure which series is the first exposure before taking any value, and must not use the transfer series (run 13), which is a later exposure. Analyses of transfer are explicitly based on runs 3 (initial learning) and 13 (initial transfer): "the following behavioral and imaging statistics reported are based on the initial learning and transfer runs (runs 3 and 13, respectively)". The plotted 'AE' point is presumably the post-rotation washout/aftereffect run, but the text never labels or analyses it, and washout ran under baseline visual feedback rather than with feedback withheld; older adults also did not fully return to baseline ("Older adults in order 1 and 2 did not return to baseline in terms of RT ... Older adults in order 2 also failed to return to baseline in terms of DE"), and a baseline-corrected analysis was run in parallel ("data without baseline correction are reported"). N discrepancy: behavioural N = 18 per age group, but "Four participants were removed from the fMRI analyses due to poor co-registration (leaving testing order 1:9 young and older adults; testing order 2:8 young and 7 older adults)" — the fMRI Ns apply to imaging only. Correlation dfs in Section 3.5 vary (df = 16, 17, 18), suggesting outlier removal in correlational analyses only.

datasets.chosen_pair_rationale: Only two age groups exist (young vs older). Within the 30° condition the first exposure belongs to presentation order 1, so the order-1 subgroups (9 older vs 9 young) are the pair; the order-2 subgroups are not used here because for them 30° was the LAST (transfer) rotation, a repeated exposure.

outcomes.measure_name: direction error (DE), degrees (primary); initial endpoint error (IEE), mm (second, alternative operationalization)
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: Older adults demonstrated a larger benefit from prior training compared to young adults in terms of reducing DE at motor transfer
outcomes.operationalization: Third (last) run of the first exposure to the 30° visual rotation for presentation order 1 (each rotation magnitude was given for three consecutive runs; runs 3–5 = A1, A2, A3 in Fig. 1). Late adaptation = the A3 point of the order-1 series. Two candidate measures are plotted for the same window: DE (Fig. 1A/B, degrees) and IEE (Fig. 1C/D, mm); RT (Fig. 1E/F) is a timing measure, not an adaptation error.

study.notes: The table detector returned no tables, but the PDF does contain Tables 1–8: Table 1 (description of SWM assessments) and Tables 2–8 (fMRI activation coordinates). None of them carry adaptation or aftereffect performance values, so none is usable for this review; all quantitative behavioural adaptation data reside in Figs. 1 and 2 only (plus supplementary Tables S1–S3, not included in this file). The text reports no group means or SDs for DE/IEE/RT during adaptation, only inferential statistics (F and t values) and the learning-percentage ranges ("mean learning percentages across conditions for older adults ranged from 9 to 27% and for young adults 33 to 64%"). The extraction pass will therefore have to work from figure series in Figs. 1 and 2 and must first determine which plotted series corresponds to the first exposure (presentation order) for each rotation magnitude; if that cannot be resolved, no value should be taken.
